# I just replaced my CV Axle and now the brakes are making scary noises

Replacing a pair of CV axles on a 2011 Toyota Corolla is a standard maintenance task, but the aftermath described here points to a classic diagnostic pitfall: assuming mechanical isolation when the issue is actually electrical. You drove the car fine immediately after installation, only for symptoms to emerge around 20 MPH with strange noises and poor stopping performance. The fact that you have already disassembled the brake system and ruled out lines or ABS sensor cables suggests you are looking at this from a purely mechanical standpoint. However, the Diagnostic Trouble Codes (DTCs) you provided reveal that the vehicle's Electronic Stability Control (VSC/TRAC) module is detecting specific circuit faults that mechanical inspection alone cannot see.

The first code, **C1413 Front Speed Sensor RH circuit output**, indicates an open or shorted condition in the wheel speed sensor circuit for the right front wheel. This is critical because the ABS and stability control systems rely on precise wheel speed data to function. When this sensor fails or loses its signal, the system cannot determine if a wheel is locking up. Consequently, the vehicle defaults to a "fail-safe" mode where ABS and traction control are disabled, but more importantly, the brake-by-wire or hydraulic assist logic may be altered by the module's internal fault flags.

The second code, **C1422 Master Cylinder Pressure Sensor Zero Point High**, is equally telling. This sensor monitors brake pressure to ensure the master cylinder is operating within its expected baseline. A "High" reading at zero pressure suggests a voltage spike or an open circuit that the ECU interprets as excessive pressure when the pedal is not pressed. This can cause the Anti-lock Braking System (ABS) pump and modulator to engage erroneously. When you press the brake pedal, the system might be fighting against its own internal logic, leading to the "weird noises" you are hearingâlikely the ABS pump cycling on and off rapidly or valves clicking as they try to compensate for phantom pressure readings.

The connection between your fresh axle installation and these codes is not necessarily that the axles caused the damage, but rather that the act of replacing them may have coincided with the failure of a component you didn't inspect closely enough, or perhaps a connector was disturbed during the job. The right front wheel speed sensor is located at the hub assembly where the new axle connects. It is highly probable that one of two things happened: either the new axle's integrated wheel speed sensor (if equipped) is faulty, or the electrical connector for the existing sensor was damaged, pushed back too far, or corroded during the removal and reinstallation process.

To resolve this, you need to verify the physical connection at the right front hub. Even if you do not see visible damage, ensure the connector is fully seated and locked. If the axle assembly includes a new wheel speed sensor integrated into the CV joint housing (common on some Corolla models), that sensor might have arrived defective. You can test the circuit continuity with a multimeter to confirm if the signal wire is open or if there is excessive resistance.

Additionally, clear the codes using your scan tool and drive the vehicle again to see if the C1422 pressure sensor code returns immediately. If it does, the issue is likely a genuine electrical fault in the master cylinder circuit rather than just a noise from the wheel hub. Addressing these electrical faults is essential; driving with disabled ABS and stability control reduces your safety margin significantly, especially in emergency stops where you need electronic assistance to prevent wheel lock-up.
